strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting a target language model’s training trajectory to support efficient hyperparameter selection. Decomposing validation loss by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective.

The experimental coverage is substantial, spanning models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, ID and OOD validation data, and additional GPT-NeoX and MoE fitting experiments. Forecasting from early training prefixes improves considerably over the three reported elementary baselines.

The data-mixture application connects forecasting to actual training outcomes. The selected mixtures achieve lower final perplexity in all four model/distribution settings and improve 12 of 14 downstream benchmark comparisons. The appendices also document architectures, training configurations, and package versions.
weaknesses: The central comparative advantage is insufficiently isolated. The proposed predictor incorporates a piecewise trajectory and the known cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the baselines fit single power, reciprocal, or logarithmic functions without that schedule information. A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same schedule and piecewise structure is needed to establish the benefit of token-position decomposition. Relevant learning-curve predictors, including the cited Luo et al. (2025), are not compared.

An important result is internally inconsistent. Section 2.3 states that the positional power-law fit obtains R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, whereas Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of the 58M checkpoints. These statements require reconciliation because they directly support the choice of the hyperbolic model.

The forecasting procedure is not sufficiently specified for faithful reproduction. Algorithm 1 leaves the outlier-removal threshold unspecified, and fitting initialization, parameter constraints, and evaluation frequency are not reported. Lines 29–30 apply calibration when the observed prefix precedes the separation point, contradicting Section 2.4, which requires observations after that point. No implementation or checkpoint-loss artifact is provided to resolve these ambiguities.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence needs stronger validation. The actual candidate mixtures, search size, proxy-training budget, and predicted versus realized losses across all five candidates are absent. The application extrapolates from 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5%, while the quantitative forecasting experiments begin at 10%. Final perplexity improvements are approximately 0.7–1.3%, without uncertainty estimates or independent training repetitions; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness across runs.

The claimed generality exceeds the forecasting evidence. Training predominantly uses one corpus and cosine schedules. The additional architectures and the linear-schedule experiment demonstrate retrospective fitting, rather than forecasting unseen trajectory segments. OOD evaluation text does not establish generalization to different training distributions or optimization settings. The supported claim is therefore narrower than a generic temporal law for decoder language models.

The theoretical interpretations need qualification. Equation 17 follows from manually freezing two fitted parameters; it does not independently establish that positional reweighting is unnecessary. The weighting experiments support competitiveness against the three tested strategies. Appendix C also rejects exponential functions by setting their additive offset to zero, although the candidate family includes a free offset and can therefore approach a nonzero loss floor.
